newsitem.title: USA: U.S. trade deficit likely to grow this year.
newsitem.headline: U.S. trade deficit likely to grow this year.

text.p: The strong dollar and rising oil imports are likely to push the nation's trade deficit, already at an eight-year-high, up further this year despite government predictions to the contrary, trade analysts said.
The Commerce Department said Wednesday the deficit rose 8.7 percent to $114.23 billion last year, the highest since a $115.5 billion gap in 1988.

Commerce Secretary William Daley blamed the rise on higher oil prices and sluggish economies in Europe and Japan, which hurt sales of American goods abroad. He predicted better days ahead for exporters as economies elsewhere improve.
"Our trade deficit numbers in '97 will be good," he told a news conference. "I think 1997 will be a good year for the economy. Our competitiveness is unquestioned in the world."
But several analysts said the trade deficit with the rest of the world was likely to grow in 1997.
"I don't see anything on the horizon that is going to cause it to narrow right away," said Cynthia Latta, senior economist with DRI/McGraw Hill.
"The strong dollar is going to bring imports in. We're going to see a nine-year high," Latta quipped when asked what she expected for the deficit this year.

The dollar rose about 8 percent against the German mark and 12 percent against the Japanese yen last year, prompting an outcry from domestic manufacturers worried about tougher competition from cheaper imports and higher prices for their products in global markets.
"A rising dollar, combined with slow growth abroad, bodes poorly for trade prospects in 1997," said Howard Lewis, vice president for trade and technology at the National Association of Manufacturers.
"Our trade deficit will persist until our major trading partners deregulate their economies to spur growth and policy makers take seriously the dangers of a stronger dollar," he said.
Economists said they expected oil imports, which rose 6.4 percent last year from 1995, to rise again this year.
"Oil imports are going to keep rising as domestic production declines," said Larry Chimerine, chief economist at the Economic Strategy Institute.

Meanwhile, Michael Fenollosa, an economist with John Hancock Financial Services, said he does not expect economic growth to pick up in Europe as projected by Clinton administration officials. Higher economic growth abroad would increase demand for American exports.
Those countries are keeping a tight lid on spending to help qualify for the planned single European currency, he said.
"That's not going to help the growth for those countries. They also have big structural labour market problems that are not going to be addressed overnight. That is going to restrain growth."
He said he also was not optimistic that Japan's economy will pick up this year. But he added that a bigger deficit does not bode ill for the economy.
"It is not a problem," said Fenollosa. Imports are keeping U.S. inflation in check while the country enjoys a low 5.3 percent unemployment rate, he said.
